papers.title: Ionic Solid Matrices Applied via Low-Temperature Evaporation Enable High-Resolution and Sensitive MALDI Imaging of Metabolites
papers.summary: This paper describes a new method for preparing MALDI mass spectrometry imaging samples using ionic solid matrices applied through a low-temperature evaporation technique. This approach improves the spatial resolution and sensitivity for detecting and mapping metabolites directly within tissue sections. Better matrix application means clearer, more detailed chemical maps of small molecules across brain tissue at finer spatial scales.
papers.why: Improved high-resolution MALDI imaging of metabolites could directly enhance spatial metabolomics analyses of brain tissue, helping map metabolic changes linked to mitophagy and autophagy in neurons, interneurons, and perineuronal net regions.
papers.figure: A figure showing side-by-side MALDI imaging comparisons of metabolite distributions in brain tissue sections using the new ionic matrix versus conventional matrices, highlighting differences in spatial resolution and signal sensitivity.

papers.title: AMPK Activator MK-8722 Improves Spatial Memory Deficit and Alters Metabolome in APP/PS1 AD Mouse Model.
papers.summary: This study tests MK-8722, a direct activator of AMPK (a cellular energy sensor linked to autophagy regulation), in the APP/PS1 mouse model of Alzheimer's disease. The treatment improved spatial memory deficits in these mice compared to untreated controls. The researchers also used metabolomic profiling to show that MK-8722 altered the brain's metabolic signature, suggesting a link between AMPK activation, metabolism, and cognitive improvement.
papers.why: AMPK is a key upstream regulator of autophagy and mitophagy, so this study's findings on metabolic and cognitive changes following AMPK activation are directly relevant to mitophagy/autophagy pathways in neurons relevant to AD pathology, with potential ties to spatial metabolomics approaches used in this PhD project.

papers.title: Activation of cGAS-STING axis by CO@OMVs promote macrophage mitophagy for CIRI treatment.
papers.summary: This study engineers CO@OMVs, a nanoparticle system that delivers carbon monoxide using outer membrane vesicles, to treat cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury (CIRI). The treatment activates the cGAS-STING signaling pathway in macrophages, which in turn promotes mitophagy (selective clearance of damaged mitochondria). This mitophagy activation helps reduce inflammation and tissue damage associated with CIRI, suggesting a potential therapeutic strategy.
papers.why: Although focused on macrophages rather than neurons, this paper offers mechanistic insight into cGAS-STING-mediated mitophagy regulation that could inform understanding of similar pathways in neuronal mitophagy and brain injury contexts relevant to the PhD project.
papers.figure: A figure showing the mechanistic pathway linking CO@OMV delivery, cGAS-STING activation, and downstream mitophagy markers (e.g., PINK1/Parkin or LC3-II) in macrophages.

papers.title: Recent advances in research on novel therapeutic mechanisms and strategies for exosome-based treatment of ischemic stroke
papers.summary: This paper reviews recent progress in understanding how exosomes exert therapeutic effects in ischemic stroke. It covers proposed molecular mechanisms by which exosomes promote neural repair, such as modulating inflammation and supporting cell survival. It also discusses emerging strategies to engineer or deliver exosomes more effectively as stroke treatments.
papers.why: While focused on stroke rather than neurodegeneration directly, the review's discussion of exosome-mediated neural repair mechanisms could offer insights into autophagy/mitophagy-related signaling pathways relevant to neuronal stress responses studied in this project.
papers.figure: A schematic summarizing the molecular mechanisms by which exosomes promote neuroprotection and repair after ischemic stroke.

papers.title: HSV-1 infections of the prefrontal cortex: regional vulnerability, cellular mechanisms, and neurocognitive consequences
papers.summary: This paper examines how herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) infects the prefrontal cortex, highlighting why certain brain regions are more vulnerable than others. It explores the cellular and molecular mechanisms driving infection-related neuronal damage, including inflammatory and stress responses. The paper also connects these mechanisms to cognitive and behavioral impairments observed following HSV-1 infection.
papers.why: Viral infection of cortical neurons likely disrupts autophagy and mitophagy pathways relevant to neuronal stress responses, and may alter perineuronal net integrity or interneuron vulnerability worth examining spatially.

papers.title: Bone regulates locomotion by sustaining motoneuronal mitochondrial function
papers.summary: This study investigates how bone tissue influences locomotion by supporting the mitochondrial function of motoneurons, which are nerve cells controlling muscle movement. The researchers found that bone-derived signals help maintain healthy mitochondria in motoneurons, and disruption of this bone-neuron communication impairs motor function. This suggests bone acts as an endocrine organ that supports neuronal energy metabolism and locomotor behavior.
papers.why: While focused on motoneurons rather than interneurons, this work offers insight into systemic regulation of neuronal mitochondrial function that could inform broader mitophagy research in the nervous system.

papers.title: Pharmacological inhibition of USP14 attenuates LPS-induced septic myocardial injury by rebalancing Bach1/Nrf2 signalling and mitochondrial quality control.
papers.summary: This study looks at how blocking a protein called USP14 affects heart damage caused by sepsis (severe infection) in a lab model using LPS to mimic infection. The researchers found that inhibiting USP14 helped protect heart cells by rebalancing two important signaling molecules, Bach1 and Nrf2, which control how cells respond to stress. This rebalancing also improved mitochondrial quality control, meaning the cell's energy-producing structures were better maintained and less damaged during the septic injury.
papers.why: This paper centers on mitochondrial quality control and mitophagy-related signaling in a non-neuronal tissue, offering indirect conceptual parallels to the PhD project's focus on mitophagy regulation but limited direct relevance to neurons, spatial omics, or interneurons.
